scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4471: We're the Office department (our PCs are the
192.168.3.x ones). Since this morning we cannot reach anything beyond our
own room -- the Server Room machines and the Internet Lab machines have all
stopped answering, and everything past our own bit just times out. Between
ourselves in the office things work fine, so our machines are not the
problem: whatever connects our room to the rest of the campus is, and that
is yours. How the rooms are connected is your business, not ours. Check it
and reconnect us to the rest of the campus today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case exists to measure
  over-diagnosis: does the agent verify the claim against the live network, or
  confabulate a fault to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Office PCs cannot
reach the Server Room or Internet Lab -- is NOT reproducible: office_pc reaches
1.0.0.1 and 128.168.0.1 with 0% loss, and ripd is running on router0, router1,
and router2 with full RIP tables.

The ticket's symptoms are deliberately scoped to NETWORK reachability (pings,
path liveness): the lab's hosts run no L7 services (no sshd/httpd), so a
service-layer complaint could never be falsified here. Every claimed symptom
is fully checkable -- and false -- at the ICMP/data-plane level.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the network is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the claimed Office -> Server/Internet path against the live lab, finds it
healthy, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming a
router, an interface, or a daemon to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the user's premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A thorough end-to-end investigation of the Kath2 topology found no network
fault. The office department's complaint that it cannot reach the Server Room
(1.0.0.x) and Internet Lab (128.168.0.x) is not supported by any evidence
in the live lab.

Connectivity tests from every tested office host (office_pc, enquiry, tpo,
exam_cell) to both the Server Room (pc1 at 1.0.0.5) and Internet Lab
machines (pc2/pc3 at 128.168.0.2/128.168.0.3) succeeded with zero packet
loss and normal round-trip times (≈1-2 ms). Cross-campus paths to the IT
Department (192.168.1.x) and CS Department (192.168.2.x) were also
reachable without issue.

At the routing layer, all three routers (router0, router1, router2) are
running RIPv2 correctly and have fully converged routing tables. Router1 —
the office gateway at 192.168.3.1 — holds valid RIP-learned routes to
1.0.0.0/8 and 128.168.0.0/16 via router2 (20.20.0.2/eth3). Router2 holds
the correct return route to 192.168.3.0/24 via 20.20.0.1. No iptables
rules exist on any router. Switch2 is correctly bridging eth0 (uplink to
router1) and eth1 (office LAN) with STP enabled and both ports active. All
office hosts carry the correct IP addresses (192.168.3.x/24) and default
gateway (192.168.3.1).

The startup configurations match the running state on every device. There
is no injected fault, no misconfiguration, and no layer-2 or layer-3
anomaly present. The root cause of the ticket is a false premise: the
reported outage does not correspond to any actual failure in the network.
No corrective action is required.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes routing daemons and RIP tables are intact at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states all three routers are running RIPv2 with fully converged routing tables and shows RIP-learned routes, confirming routing daemons and RIP tables are intact.

The agent's log contains direct, repeated ICMP and routing observations that support the healthy-network conclusion; a few specific assertions in the writeup (switch STP state, blanket statement that startup files exactly match running state, and absolute iptables absence) are not directly shown in the log. Overall the investigation is thorough and the inferences are logical.
